items.prompt: What does line coverage tell you about a line?
choices: That a test checked its result
That some test made it run
That the line is free of bugs
items.explanation: Coverage records execution only. It says nothing about whether any test inspected what the line produced.

items.prompt: A test calls a function but never checks the return value. Is the function's code covered?
choices: No, an unchecked call does not count
Only if the function has one line
Yes, its lines still ran
items.explanation: Coverage tools count lines that execute, whether or not anything is asserted about the output.

items.prompt: Which question does mutation testing ask?
choices: Would any test fail if this code were wrong?
How many lines did the tests execute overall?
Is every public function fully documented?
items.explanation: It plants a small bug on purpose and watches whether the suite notices.

items.prompt: Which signal measures execution, not verification?
choices: Mutation score
Line coverage
Number of failed mutants
items.explanation: Coverage counts what ran. Mutation score is the one that probes whether tests would detect a change.

items.prompt: In the shipping example, coverage was 100% and the mutation score was 50%. What does the gap show?
choices: The tool measured the coverage wrongly, so the 100% is unreliable
Half the lines never ran at all in the suite
Many lines ran without their results being checked
items.explanation: All lines ran, which is why coverage was full. The score dropped because half the planted bugs went unnoticed.

items.prompt: Full coverage proves which of these?
choices: Every line ran at least once
Every branch is correct for all inputs
No bug can ever reach production
items.explanation: It proves execution happened, nothing about correctness or detection power.

items.prompt: A line runs in a test, but no assertion depends on its output. Is a bug there detected?
choices: Yes, running it is enough
No, nothing would fail
Yes, if the test is long
items.explanation: Detection needs an assertion that depends on the line's effect. Merely running it detects nothing.

items.prompt: Which phrase best contrasts the two ideas?
choices: Fast
Old versus new
Ran versus would notice
items.explanation: Coverage says the line ran. Mutation testing says whether a failure would be noticed.

items.prompt: A suite reports 100% line coverage. A planted change flipping `>` to `>=` in a pricing rule leaves every test green. What is the best reading of this?
choices: The coverage tool mis-reported and the line never executed
The tests run that line but none checks the value at the edge
The tests are failing silently, so the green result is invalid
The mutant was equivalent, so nothing should have failed
items.explanation: The line ran, so coverage is honest. What is missing is an assertion that depends on the value where `>` and `>=` differ.
items.reference:
Two questions, two tools
📏 coverage asks: did this line run?
🔎 mutation testing asks: would a test fail if it were wrong?
🕳️ a line can run and never be checked
📊 full coverage can sit beside a weak suite
Why: coverage counts execution, and only a deliberately planted bug shows whether anything verifies the result.
items.learnMore:
Running is not checking

A test that calls a function and ignores the result still marks every line it touched as covered. Coverage cannot see what the test failed to assert.

Common mistake

Treating a high coverage number as proof the suite would catch a regression.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist you tick through at work or home. Where have you ticked an item as done without confirming the result was right?

items.prompt: Two suites both reach 100% coverage on the same function. Suite A asserts exact outputs, suite B only calls the function. Which statement is correct?
choices: Coverage cannot distinguish them, mutation testing can
Coverage ranks suite A higher because it asserts more than B
Mutation testing cannot tell them apart either, only humans can
Suite B scores higher because it runs faster than A
items.explanation: Both execute the same lines, so coverage is identical. Planted bugs would fail suite A's assertions and slip past suite B.

No, coverage above 90% is meaningless as a signal

choices: Adding a test that asserts an exact output at a threshold
Adding a test that checks an error is raised for bad input
Adding a test that calls an untested function and asserts nothing
Replacing a vague assertion with an exact expected value
items.explanation: The empty call executes new lines, so the number rises, yet nothing can fail when those lines are wrong.

items.prompt: What is a mutant?
choices: A test that fails on purpose
A copy with one small change
A bug that a customer found in production
items.explanation: A tool makes a tiny deliberate change to create it, one change per mutant.

items.prompt: A test fails against a mutant. What is the mutant called?
choices: Survived
Equivalent
Killed
items.explanation: A failing test means the suite caught the planted bug.

items.prompt: Every test passes against a mutant. What is it called?
choices: Survived
Killed
Covered
items.explanation: If nothing fails, the suite did not notice the change.

items.prompt: How is the mutation score computed?
choices: Passing tests divided by all tests in the suite
Killed over total mutants
Covered lines divided by all lines in the file
items.explanation: It is the share of planted bugs the suite caught.

items.prompt: 4 mutants are made and 2 are killed. What is the score?
items.explanation: 2 divided by 4 is 0.5, which is 50%.

items.prompt: Does a surviving mutant mean the original code is broken?
choices: No, it means the tests have a gap
Yes, the original has the same bug
Yes, but only in production
items.explanation: The original is never changed. A survivor describes the tests.

items.prompt: Who usually creates mutants?
choices: A reviewer, by hand
A tool, mechanically
The customer, by reporting
items.explanation: Tools apply small rules automatically so thousands can be tried quickly.

items.prompt: Is a high mutation score a good sign?
choices: No, it means many tests had to fail on purpose
No, it means many lines ran
Yes, most planted bugs were caught
items.explanation: A high score means the suite noticed most of the injected mistakes.

items.prompt: A tool generates 12 mutants. 9 are killed, 1 is equivalent and excluded, 2 survive. What is the score on non-equivalent mutants?
choices: 9 of 12, exactly 75%
9 of 11, about 82%
9 of 10, exactly 90%
2 of 11, about 18%
items.explanation: The equivalent mutant leaves the denominator, so 9 killed out of the 11 that could be killed. 9/11 is about 0.82.
items.reference:
Reading a mutation run
🧬 mutant = code with one small deliberate change
💥 killed = a test failed, the suite noticed
🕳️ survived = every test passed, a gap exists
➗ score = killed divided by total mutants
Why: a mutant is a probe of the tests: if nothing fails, the suite could not see that exact bug.
items.learnMore:
The verdict is about the tests

The original code is never altered during the run. A survivor shows that the suite would not notice that specific mistake if it were introduced.

Common mistake

Reading a survivor as proof that the current code is broken.
items.reflection: Imagine a smoke alarm you test by waving smoke at it. If it stays silent, what is the faulty thing, the room or the alarm?

items.prompt: After a run, one mutant survived. Which action best follows?
choices: Inspect that line and decide if a test can tell
Delete the line from the production code to be safe
Rerun the tool until the mutant is killed by chance
Mark the original code as failing code review
items.explanation: A survivor points to an exact spot and kind of change. The next step is judging whether a test should catch it.

choices: The production code has this exact bug today
The whole suite is now complete and finished
The mutant must be an equivalent one
The suite can detect that specific change
items.explanation: A kill shows only that this one mutation is caught, not that the function is correct or the suite finished.

items.prompt: Two suites face the same 10 mutants. Suite X kills 6 and suite Y kills 8. What can you say?
choices: X is stronger since it has fewer failing tests
They are equal because both ran every line
Y caught more of these planted bugs, so Y looks stronger here
Y has fewer tests, so it must be weaker
items.explanation: Same mutants, more kills means more detection power on those probes.

items.prompt: What is a mutation operator?
choices: A person who starts and runs the tool
A rule for one kind of change
A test that checks a numeric limit
items.explanation: Each operator describes one kind of change, such as flipping a comparison.

items.prompt: Which change is a conditional boundary mutation?
choices: Deleting a comment
Renaming a variable
Changing `>` to `>=`
items.explanation: It moves the exact edge where the condition flips.

items.prompt: Which change is an arithmetic replacement?
choices: Changing `+` to `-`
Changing `>` to `>=`
Deleting a whole line
items.explanation: It swaps one arithmetic operator for another.

items.prompt: What does a statement-removal mutation do?
choices: Renames a function
Deletes a line
Adds a new test
items.explanation: It checks whether the suite notices the line is gone.

items.prompt: What does a return-value mutation do?
choices: Changes how fast it runs under load
Changes the names of the tests
Changes what a function returns
items.explanation: For example it returns 0 or a negated value.

items.prompt: Do operators model real human mistakes?
choices: Yes, common small slips
No, purely random damage
No, only syntax errors
items.explanation: They are chosen to resemble plausible off-by-one, sign, and forgotten-line mistakes.

items.prompt: Which operator asks whether a test sits exactly on a threshold?
choices: Statement removal
Conditional boundary
Return value
items.explanation: Only an exact-edge input tells the two comparison versions apart.

items.prompt: Are the operators independent probes?
choices: No, they all test one single thing
No, only the very first one matters
Yes, each asks its own question
items.explanation: A suite can pass one kind of probe and fail another.

items.prompt: A suite kills all 8 arithmetic mutants and 0 of 5 boundary mutants. Which description fits?
choices: It is strong everywhere because arithmetic is the hardest case
It checks computed numbers but never tests exact thresholds
It has no tests for numbers at all, only for text
All five boundary mutants must be equivalent ones
items.explanation: Separate operators probe separate habits. Perfect arithmetic kills and zero boundary kills means no test lands on an edge.
items.reference:
One operator, one question
🎯 boundary: is anything exactly on the threshold?
➕ arithmetic: is the computed number checked?
🗑️ statement removal: would a missing line be noticed?
↩️ return value: is the result inspected?
Why: each operator models one common human mistake, so each asks the suite a different narrow question.
items.learnMore:
Operators are independent probes

Strength against one kind of mistake says nothing about another. Reading results per operator shows which kind of check is missing.

Common mistake

Averaging every operator into one percentage and missing a zero in a single row.
items.reflection: Think of a proofreader who only checks spelling. Which other kinds of mistake would sail past them, and which operator-like checks would you add?

items.prompt: Which mutation is most likely to expose a missing test for an off-by-one limit?
choices: Changing `<` to `<=` in the limit check
Reordering two unrelated lines in the file
Renaming a local variable to a clearer name
Changing the wording of a log message
items.explanation: Only a boundary mutation moves the edge by one, and only an on-the-edge test notices.

items.explanation: If the result could become zero without any failure, nothing asserts on what comes back.

Arithmetic replacement, since a sign was swapped
Statement removal, since no test depends on the call
Return value, since the output was never inspected
items.explanation: The mutation deleted a statement. Survival means no test depends on that side effect.

items.prompt: How many suite runs does a tool need for 50 mutants?
items.explanation: Each mutant needs one full run of the suite.

items.prompt: What is total time if there are 10 mutants and a run takes 3 seconds?
choices: 13 seconds
3 seconds
30 seconds
items.explanation: 10 runs of 3 seconds each is 30 seconds.

items.prompt: Which factor makes a mutation run longer?
choices: More mutants
Fewer mutants
A shorter suite
items.explanation: More mutants means more suite runs.

items.prompt: Which factor also makes it longer?
choices: A faster test suite
A slower test suite
A smaller module
items.explanation: Each of the runs takes more time when one run is slower.

items.prompt: Where is mutation testing usually run?
choices: After every keystroke
Only once ever
Nightly or weekly
items.explanation: Its cost suits a scheduled job rather than the inner loop.

items.prompt: Which code is a good target for scoping?
choices: Pricing or permission logic
Placeholder text on a page
Color constants in a theme
items.explanation: Critical modules justify the extra cost because silent bugs there are expensive.

items.prompt: Is the survivor list usually a merge gate?
choices: Yes, always on every change
No, it guides new tests
Yes, for every typo
items.explanation: Teams use it diagnostically, not as a per-change blocker.

items.prompt: If you double the mutants and keep suite time fixed, total time does what?
choices: Stays the same
Halves
Doubles
items.explanation: Total is mutants times time per run, so it scales with mutants.

items.prompt: A module generates 200 mutants and one suite run takes 30 seconds. About how long is the full run?
choices: 6.7 minutes
100 minutes
30 minutes
200 minutes
items.explanation: 200 times 30 seconds is 6000 seconds, which is 100 minutes.
items.reference:
Total time is a product
⏱️ total = mutants x time of one suite run
📈 doubling either factor doubles the total
🎯 so scope to critical modules
🌙 and run nightly or weekly, not per commit
Why: every mutant needs its own full suite run, so the cost multiplies rather than adds.
items.learnMore:
Multiplying two growing numbers

A bigger module makes more mutants, and a bigger suite makes each run longer. Both grow with the codebase, so the product outgrows any per-commit time budget.

Common mistake

Putting a slow, exhaustive check in the inner loop where a fast one belongs.
items.reflection: Think of a thorough inspection you could do on everything but afford only on the most important thing. How would you decide what counts as most important?

items.prompt: A team halves the suite time but the module is refactored and now produces three times the mutants. What happens to total time?
choices: It grows to 1.5 times the original
It drops to half of the original
It stays exactly the same as before
It triples compared with the original
items.explanation: The factor is 3 times 0.5, which equals 1.5, so the total rises to 1.5 times the original.

items.prompt: The rule is 'over 20 kg gets a surcharge'. Is exactly 20 kg surcharged?
choices: Yes
No
Only at checkout
items.explanation: 'Over' means strictly greater than 20.

items.prompt: Which input can tell `weight > 20` from `weight >= 20`?
choices: Exactly 2
Exactly 100
Exactly 20
items.explanation: Both versions agree everywhere except on the edge value.

items.prompt: A test uses 25 kg. Does it kill the `>=` mutant?
choices: No, both versions agree at 25
Yes, always
Yes, if the fee is large enough
items.explanation: 25 is past the edge, so it takes the same branch either way.

items.prompt: What was the mutation score before the boundary tests were added?
items.explanation: 2 of the 4 mutants were killed.

items.prompt: What was the score after the boundary tests were added?
items.explanation: Both surviving mutants were killed, so 4 of 4.

items.prompt: What happened to line coverage after adding them?
choices: Nothing, it stayed 100%
It rose to 100%
It dropped to 50%
items.explanation: Every line already ran, so coverage had nothing left to show.

items.prompt: What is the fee for 20 kg and 10 km in the example?
items.explanation: 5 plus 10 plus 1 is 16, with no surcharge at exactly 20.

items.prompt: What do boundary mutants need to be killed?
choices: A very long and detailed test
A test far above the threshold
A test exactly on the threshold
items.explanation: Only the edge input distinguishes the two comparisons.

items.prompt: Distance discount applies at 500 km or more. A mutant changes `>= 500` to `> 500`. Which new test kills it?
choices: Distance 600, expecting the discounted fee
Distance 500, expecting the discounted fee
Distance 499, expecting the full fee
Distance 1000, expecting the discounted fee
items.explanation: At 500 the original discounts and the mutant does not. 499 and 600 behave the same under both.
items.reference:
Where tests land matters
🔢 threshold: over 20 kg gets the surcharge
📍 2 kg and 25 kg both sit away from the line
🧪 20 kg is the only input that tells > from >=
✅ exact-threshold test kills the mutant
Why: only an input exactly on the threshold gives different results under the original and the mutant comparison.
items.learnMore:
Away from the edge, both versions agree

A value comfortably past a threshold follows the same branch either way the comparison is written. Only the value on the edge separates them.

Common mistake

Adding more tests far from the threshold and expecting the boundary to be covered.
items.reflection: Think of a rule with a cut-off, such as an age limit or a deadline. Which exact value would reveal whether the rule means 'up to' or 'before'?

Yes, 100 kg exercises the surcharge
items.explanation: For 19, 21, and 100 the two comparisons give identical branches, so the mutant survives.

Coverage tools skip every edge case by design

The surviving mutants were removed from the count
items.explanation: The old suite already executed every line. What changed was what the tests check, which coverage does not measure.

🔢 threshold: over 20 kg gets the surcharge
📍 2 kg and 25 kg both sit away from the line
🧪 20 kg is the only input that tells > from >=
✅ exact-threshold test kills the mutant
Why: only an input exactly on the threshold gives different results under the original and the mutant comparison.
items.learnMore:
Away from the edge, both versions agree

A value comfortably past a threshold follows the same branch either way the comparison is written. Only the value on the edge separates them.

Common mistake

Adding more tests far from the threshold and expecting the boundary to be covered.

items.prompt: What is an equivalent mutant?
choices: A change that every test kills at once
A change that never alters behavior
A change that breaks the whole build
items.explanation: Its code looks different but returns the same results for all inputs.

items.prompt: Can any test kill an equivalent mutant?
choices: Yes, with enough tests
Yes, with a long test
No
items.explanation: If behavior is identical, no test can see a difference.

items.prompt: Is `a + b` to `b + a` usually equivalent?
choices: Yes, addition gives the same result
No, the order matters
No, it always crashes
items.explanation: Swapping the operands of addition does not change the sum.

items.prompt: Should every survivor become a new test?
choices: Yes, every one
No, some are equivalent
Yes, the equivalent ones first
items.explanation: A person reviews survivors and dismisses the equivalent ones.

items.prompt: How are equivalent mutants counted in the score?
choices: Counted as killed mutants
Counted as covered lines
Excluded or flagged for review
items.explanation: Leaving them in would unfairly lower the score.

items.prompt: Why do equivalent survivors cost time?
choices: A person must review each one
They slow down every single test
They break the build
items.explanation: Deciding they are harmless needs human judgment.

items.prompt: Can a tool perfectly detect equivalent mutants?
choices: Yes, always
No, in general it cannot
Yes, in under a second
items.explanation: Proving two programs behave the same is undecidable in general.

items.prompt: A survivor changes a variable name only. Is it likely a real gap?
choices: Yes, always
Yes, but only inside tests
No, behavior is unchanged
items.explanation: A pure rename cannot affect results.

items.prompt: Which mutation is most likely equivalent for the sum `base + weight + distance`?
choices: Changing the first `+` to a `-` in the sum
Reordering the operands of the additions
Deleting the whole line that computes it
Replacing the final result with a constant 0
items.explanation: Addition is commutative, so reordering leaves every result the same, unlike the other changes.

🧬 mutant changes the text of the code
🟰 but never changes what it returns
🙈 no test can kill it, however good
👀 a person reviews survivors to tell them apart
Why: if behavior is identical for every input, no test can differ, so the survivor is noise and not a gap.
items.learnMore:
Why no tool can filter them all

Deciding whether two programs behave the same on every input is undecidable in general. That is why survivors need a human look before anyone writes a test.

Common mistake

Opening a ticket to write a test for every survivor automatically.
items.reflection: Think of two instructions worded differently that always lead to the same result. How would you convince yourself they never differ?

Definitely a gap, since the operator itself was changed
Definitely killed by any test that runs the loop
Impossible, since a boundary can never be equivalent
items.explanation: Both conditions stop the loop at exactly the same iteration here, so nothing observable differs.
